definition: ELIZA is an early natural language processing computer program developed from 1964 to 1967 at MIT by Joseph Weizenbaum.
details: Created to explore communication between humans and machines, ELIZA simulated conversation by using a pattern matching and substitution methodology that gave users an illusion of understanding on the part of the program, but gave no response that could be considered really understanding what was being said by either party. Whereas the ELIZA program itself was written (originally) in MAD-SLIP, the pattern matching directives that contained most of its language capability were provided in separate "scripts", represented in a Lisp-like expression. The most famous script, DOCTOR, simulated a psychotherapist of the Rogerian school (in which the therapist often reflects back the patient's words to the patient), and used rules, dictated in the script, to respond with non-directional questions to user inputs. As such, ELIZA was one of the first chatbots (originally "chatterbots") and one of the first programs capable of attempting the Turing test. Weizenbaum intended the program as a method to explore communication between humans and machines. explainer.lead: ELIZA was an early chatbot built at MIT by Joseph Weizenbaum between 1964 and 1967. Its pattern-based replies could feel surprisingly human, showing how easily a conversation can create an impression of understanding.

tiers.eli5: ELIZA is like a toy that answers by spotting a few words and rearranging what you said. Its best-known script, DOCTOR, acted like a therapist who asks you to say more instead of giving advice. It could sound thoughtful, but it did not actually understand you.
tiers.practitioner: An ELIZA-style system is implemented as pattern-matching and substitution rules, with conversational behavior kept in scripts separate from the core program. DOCTOR used this setup to produce reflective, non-directional questions. The main pitfalls are brittle, rule-dependent replies and users reading more understanding into the output than the system possesses.
tiers.paperLevel: ELIZA maps an input string to an output string through script-defined pattern matching and substitution, without a mechanism that genuinely understands either participant's statements. Weizenbaum developed the original program in MAD-SLIP at MIT from 1964 to 1967, with language directives represented in separate Lisp-like scripts. Its fluent-seeming exchanges therefore demonstrate conversational imitation rather than semantic comprehension.

explainer.example: If a user writes, "I am unhappy with my mother," a DOCTOR-style rule could notice the reference to the user's mother and reply, "Tell me more about your mother." The reply continues the exchange by reusing the input, not by understanding the family situation.

usedIn.name: DOCTOR script
usedIn.detail: ELIZA's most famous script simulated a Rogerian psychotherapist by reflecting users' words and asking non-directional questions.

usedIn.name: Human–machine communication research
usedIn.detail: Weizenbaum created ELIZA to explore how people and machines communicate.

usedIn.name: Early chatbot and Turing-test work
usedIn.detail: ELIZA was one of the first chatbots and one of the first programs capable of attempting the Turing test.

explainer.intuition: ELIZA works like a set of conversational fill-in-the-blank cards: recognize a familiar shape in someone's sentence, rearrange part of it, and return a prompt. This can sustain the feeling of a conversation without requiring the program to grasp its meaning.
howItWorks: The program uses directives from a separate script to look for matching patterns.
Substitution rules transform matched parts of the input into material for a response.
With DOCTOR, the response typically reflects the user's wording or asks a non-directional question.
explainer.whyItMatters: ELIZA became an early landmark in chatbots and human–machine communication. Weizenbaum was surprised when some users, including his secretary, attributed human-like feelings to it, revealing a gap between convincing conversation and actual understanding.
misconceptions: ELIZA did not truly understand what either the user or the program was saying.
DOCTOR was a script supplying language rules, not a separate name for the entire underlying program.
Being capable of attempting the Turing test does not mean that ELIZA passed it.
